title: Chemical Bonding & Molecular Structure Test - 4 (Topic Test)

test.description: Back Bonding and Bridge Bonding, Dipole Moment

en.content: Which of the following is correct order of Lewis acid strength?
en.explanation:
1. Comparing Halides with the Same Central Atom

○ When evaluating molecules like $\mathrm{BF_3}$, $\mathrm{BCl_3}$, $\mathrm{BBr_3}$, and $\mathrm{BI_3}$, Boron acts as the central atom in all of them.

○ In $\mathrm{BF_3}$, Boron has an empty $2p$ orbital, and Fluorine has a lone pair of electrons in its $2p$ orbital.

○ Because these orbitals are similar in size ($2p\pi - 2p\pi$ overlap), Fluorine can effectively back-donate its electrons to Boron.

○ This back-bonding partially completes Boron's octet, reducing its need to accept external electron pairs and making it a relatively weak Lewis acid.

○ In contrast, a molecule like $\mathrm{BI_3}$ involves Boron's $2p$ orbital and Iodine's much larger $5p$ orbital.

○ Due to the poor size compatibility between the $2p$ and $5p$ orbitals, the extent of orbital overlap is very weak, resulting in negligible back-bonding.

○ Because Boron does not receive internal electron density in $\mathrm{BI_3}$, it remains highly electron-deficient and acts as a stronger Lewis acid.

○ Therefore, the correct order of acidic strength is:

$$\mathrm{BF_3 < BCl_3 < BBr_3 < BI_3}$$

○ This logic eliminates options (1) and (2) because they present the reverse trend.

  1. Comparing Halides with Different Central Atoms

○ To evaluate the remaining options, we compare molecules with the same halogen but different central atoms, such as $\mathrm{BCl_3}$ and $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$.

○ Both Boron and Aluminum possess a $+3$ oxidation state in these molecules.

○ However, Boron has a much smaller atomic size than Aluminum.

○ Because the same charge is distributed over a smaller volume, Boron has a significantly higher charge density.

○ This higher charge density gives Boron a much stronger ability to attract an incoming electron pair (a Lewis base).

○ Consequently, Boron-based halides have a higher Lewis acidic strength than their Aluminum-based counterparts.

○ This confirms that $\mathrm{BCl_3 > AlCl_3}$ is a correct statement, while $\mathrm{AlF_3 > BF_3}$ is incorrect.

Final Answer

The correct option is (C) $\mathrm{BCl_3 > AlCl_3}$.

hi.content: निम्नलिखित में से लुईस अम्ल सामर्थ्य का सही क्रम कौन सा है?

options.content: the hybridization of the central atom always changes.
the bond angle, involving the central atom always changes.
the bond order and bond strength always increase.

en.explanation:
Option A: the hybridization of the central atom always changes.

  • False. While back bonding can change hybridization, it does not always do so.

  • Example where it changes: In trisilylamine, $N(SiH_3)_3$, the lone pair on nitrogen is donated into the empty $d$-orbitals of silicon. This delocalization causes the nitrogen atom to become planar ($sp^2$ hybridized) instead of the expected pyramidal ($sp^3$) shape.

  • Example where it doesn't change: In boron trifluoride ($BF_3$), the boron atom undergoes $sp^2$ hybridization and remains trigonal planar. The $p\pi-p\pi$ back bonding from fluorine to boron creates partial double bond character but does not alter the $sp^2$ hybridization state.

Option B: the bond angle, involving the central atom always changes.

  • False. In highly symmetrical molecules, back bonding does not affect the bond angle.

  • Example: In $BF_3$, despite the back bonding from the fluorine atoms to the central boron atom, the molecule remains perfectly symmetric and trigonal planar. The F-B-F bond angles remain exactly $120^\circ$.

Option C: the bond order and bond strength always increase.

  • True. Back bonding is essentially the formation of a coordinate $\pi$-bond alongside an existing $\sigma$-bond. The donation of electron density from a filled orbital to an empty orbital on an adjacent atom creates partial double bond character.

  • Because extra electron density is shared between the two nuclei, the bond order always increases (e.g., the B-F bond order in $BF_3$ is approximately 1.33 instead of 1). An increase in bond order inherently results in a stronger bond (higher bond enthalpy) and a shorter bond length.

Option D: Lewis acid strength increases always.

  • False. It actually decreases the Lewis acid strength.

  • A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor (meaning it has a vacant orbital). When back bonding occurs, an adjacent atom donates its own lone pair into that vacant orbital, partially satisfying the central atom's electron deficiency internally.

  • Example: Because fluorine is highly effective at $2p\pi-2p\pi$ back bonding with boron, $BF_3$ has its electron deficiency partially resolved internally. Therefore, it has less tendency to accept external electrons compared to $BI_3$, making $BF_3$ a much weaker Lewis acid than expected.

Correct Option:

The correct choice is Option C, as the formation of a partial $\pi$-bond through back bonding will inherently always increase both the bond order and the bond strength.

en.content: In which of the following bond angle around underline atom is 120o?
en.explanation:
Answer: Option B — N(GeH₃)₃

In N(CH₃)₃, nitrogen is $sp^3$ hybridised. It has three bond pairs and one lone pair, so the shape is pyramidal. Because of lone pair–bond pair repulsion, the C–N–C angle is close to $108^\circ$, not $120^\circ$.

In N(GeH₃)₃, the situation is different. Germanium has vacant $d$ orbitals available. The lone pair on nitrogen is donated into these empty $d$ orbitals of Ge, giving $p\pi$–$d\pi$ back bonding. Once the lone pair is used up in this way, nitrogen no longer keeps it as a localised lone pair. Nitrogen then becomes $sp^2$ hybridised, and the molecule turns out planar triangular with

$$\angle \text{Ge–N–Ge} = 120^\circ$$

This is exactly the same reason why trisilylamine, N(SiH₃)₃, is planar while trimethylamine is pyramidal.

In P(CH₃)₃, phosphorus is $sp^3$ hybridised with a lone pair. Since carbon has no vacant $d$ orbitals, no back bonding is possible. The molecule stays pyramidal with an angle even smaller than $109.5^\circ$ (about $99^\circ$), because phosphorus is a larger atom and its lone pair pushes the bonds closer.

In P(SiH₃)₃, although Si has vacant $d$ orbitals, phosphorus is a big atom and its $3p$ orbital does not overlap effectively with the $3d$ orbital of silicon. So back bonding is very poor here, the lone pair remains on P, and the molecule is pyramidal, not planar.

So only in N(GeH₃)₃ does the central atom become $sp^2$ hybridised and give a bond angle of $120^\circ$.

en.content: The incorrect statement regarding O(SiH3)2 and OCl2 molecule is/are :

options.content: The strength of back bonding is more in O(SiH3)2 molecule than OCl2 molecule
Si — Ô — Si bond angle in O(SiH3)2 is greater than Cl — Ô — Cl bond angle in OCl2
The nature of back bond in both molecules is (2pπ - 3dπ)
Hybridisation of central O-atom in both molecules is same

en.explanation:
In $\text{O(SiH}_3)_2$, the central oxygen atom has filled $2p$ orbitals containing lone pairs, while the silicon atoms have empty $3d$ orbitals. Due to effective orbital overlap, oxygen donates its lone pairs to the empty $3d$ orbitals of silicon. This forms a strong $(2p_\pi - 3d_\pi)$ back bond. Because of this delocalization, the steric number of oxygen decreases from $4$ to $3$, changing the hybridization of oxygen to $sp^2$. The $\text{Si}-\hat{\text{O}}-\text{Si}$ bond angle increases significantly to about $144^\circ$.

In $\text{OCl}_2$, chlorine also has vacant $3d$ orbitals, so any back-bonding is of $(2p_\pi - 3d_\pi)$ type. However, chlorine is highly electronegative and relatively larger, making back-bonding extremely weak. As a result, the lone pairs remain predominantly on the oxygen atom. Oxygen stays $sp^3$ hybridized, and the $\text{Cl}-\hat{\text{O}}-\text{Cl}$ bond angle is around $111^\circ$.

Now let us check the given options:

  • Option A is correct because the back-bonding between $\text{O}$ and $\text{Si}$ is much stronger than between $\text{O}$ and $\text{Cl}$.

  • Option B is correct because the bond angle in $\text{O(SiH}_3)_2$ ($\approx 144^\circ$) is greater than in $\text{OCl}_2$ ($\approx 111^\circ$).

  • Option C is correct because in both cases, the filled orbital of oxygen is $2p$ and the vacant orbital of the surrounding atom is $3d$, forming a $(2p_\pi - 3d_\pi)$ bond.

  • Option D is incorrect because the hybridization of oxygen in $\text{O(SiH}_3)_2$ is $sp^2$, whereas in $\text{OCl}_2$ it is $sp^3$.

Therefore, the incorrect statement is Option D.

en.content: The experimental value for the dipole moment of $A-B$ bond having $\%$ ionic character of $30 \%$ is m. Find 10m. [given, bond length of $A-B=0.333 \mathrm{~nm}$ ]
en.explanation:
For a bond, percentage ionic character is given by

$$ \% \text{ ionic character}=\frac{\text{observed dipole moment}}{\text{dipole moment for }100\%\text{ ionic bond}}\times 100 $$

For a completely ionic bond,

$$ \mu = e \times r $$

In Debye, we use the relation:

$$ \mu_{\text{ionic}} = 4.8 \times r(\text{in } \mathring{A}) $$

Given bond length:

$$ 0.333 \text{ nm} = 3.33 \mathring{A} $$

So,

$$ \mu_{\text{ionic}} = 4.8 \times 3.33 $$

$$ \mu_{\text{ionic}} = 15.984 \text{ D} $$

The bond has $30\%$ ionic character, so the experimental dipole moment is

$$ m = \frac{30}{100} \times 15.984 $$

$$ m = 4.7952 \text{ D} $$

Hence,

$$ 10m = 47.952 \approx 48 $$

So, the value of $10m$ is

$$ \boxed{48} $$

en.content:
Number of compounds from the following with non-zero dipole moment is

$\mathrm{HF}, \mathrm{HI}, \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}, \mathrm{CCl}_4, \mathrm{XeF}_4, \mathrm{BF}_3, \mathrm{NF}_3, \mathrm{CHCl}_3$
en.explanation:
1. $\mathrm{HF}$: It is a linear heteronuclear diatomic molecule. Due to the high electronegativity difference between hydrogen and fluorine, it has a permanent net dipole moment. So, $\mu \neq 0$.

  2. $\mathrm{HI}$: Similar to $\mathrm{HF}$, it is a diatomic molecule with an electronegativity difference between hydrogen and iodine. So, $\mu \neq 0$.

  3. $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}$: Sulfur has two bond pairs and two lone pairs of electrons, giving the molecule a bent or V-shape (similar to $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$). The individual $\mathrm{S-H}$ bond dipoles and the lone pair contributions do not cancel each other. So, $\mu \neq 0$.

  4. $\mathrm{CCl}_4$: Carbon is bonded to four identical chlorine atoms in a symmetrical regular tetrahedral geometry. The four $\mathrm{C-Cl}$ bond dipoles point symmetrically in 3D space and completely cancel each other out. So, $\mu = 0$.

  5. $\mathrm{XeF}_4$: Xenon has four bond pairs and two lone pairs ($sp^3d^2$ hybridisation). The four fluorine atoms form a symmetrical square planar geometry, and the two lone pairs are oriented opposite to each other. All individual dipoles cancel out completely. So, $\mu = 0$.

  6. $\mathrm{BF}_3$: Boron forms three $\mathrm{B-F}$ bonds arranged symmetrically in a trigonal planar geometry at bond angles of $120^\circ$. The resultant of any two bond dipoles is equal and opposite to the third bond dipole, leading to complete cancellation. So, $\mu = 0$.

  7. $\mathrm{NF}_3$: Nitrogen has three bond pairs and one lone pair, giving it a trigonal pyramidal shape. Because of this unsymmetrical shape, the bond dipoles and the lone pair moment do not cancel out completely. So, $\mu \neq 0$.

  8. $\mathrm{CHCl}_3$: It has a tetrahedral geometry, but the four groups attached to carbon are not identical (three chlorine atoms and one hydrogen atom). Because the $\mathrm{C-H}$ and $\mathrm{C-Cl}$ bond dipoles have different magnitudes, they do not cancel each other out. So, $\mu \neq 0$.

The molecules with a non-zero dipole moment are $\mathrm{HF}$, $\mathrm{HI}$, $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}$, $\mathrm{NF}_3$, and $\mathrm{CHCl}_3$.

The total number of compounds with a non-zero dipole moment is $5$.

en.content: Among the given compounds/molecules, 1, 1-dichloro ethene, cis-1, 2-dichloroethene, trans-1,2-dichloroethene, 1, 4-dichlorobenzene, trans-2, 3-dichloro-2-butene, cis-1, 2-dichloro-1-butene, trans-2-butene, cis-3-hexene. The total number of molecules which have zero dipole moment is/are…….
en.explanation:
A molecule has zero dipole moment when its bond dipoles cancel each other due to symmetry.

Check each compound:

  • $1,1$-dichloroethene: $\mathrm{CH_2=CCl_2}$

    Both chlorine atoms are on the same carbon. The dipoles do not cancel.

    So, $\mu \neq 0$.

  • cis-$1,2$-dichloroethene: $\mathrm{CHCl=CHCl}$

    The two $\mathrm{C-Cl}$ bond dipoles are on the same side, so they add up.

    So, $\mu \neq 0$.

  • trans-$1,2$-dichloroethene: $\mathrm{CHCl=CHCl}$

    The two $\mathrm{C-Cl}$ bond dipoles are opposite and equal, so they cancel.

    So, $\mu = 0$.

  • $1,4$-dichlorobenzene

    The two chlorine atoms are at para positions. Their dipoles are equal and opposite.

    So, $\mu = 0$.

  • trans-$2,3$-dichloro-$2$-butene: $\mathrm{CH_3C(Cl)=C(Cl)CH_3}$

    The molecule is symmetrical, and the dipoles cancel.

    So, $\mu = 0$.

  • cis-$1,2$-dichloro-$1$-butene

    The chlorine atoms are on the same side and the molecule is not symmetrical.

    So, $\mu \neq 0$.

  • trans-$2$-butene: $\mathrm{CH_3CH=CHCH_3}$

    The molecule is symmetrical. Bond dipoles cancel.

    So, $\mu = 0$.

  • cis-$3$-hexene

    The molecule is cis, so the bond dipoles do not cancel completely.

    So, $\mu \neq 0$.

Thus, the molecules having zero dipole moment are:

$$ \text{trans-}1,2\text{-dichloroethene} $$

$$ 1,4\text{-dichlorobenzene} $$

$$ \text{trans-}2,3\text{-dichloro-}2\text{-butene} $$

$$ \text{trans-}2\text{-butene} $$

So, the total number of molecules with zero dipole moment is

$$ \boxed{4} $$

en.content:
Each of the following options contains a set of four molecules.

(a) BeCl$_2$, CO$_2$, BCl$_3$, CHCl$_3$

(b) SO$_2$, C$_6$H$_5$Cl, H$_2$Se, BrF$_5$

(c) BF$_3$, O$_3$, SF$_6$, XeF$_6$

(d) NO$_2$, NH$_3$, POCl$_3$, CH$_3$Cl

$X =$ Total number of molecules which possess permanent dipole moment at room temperature. So, the value of $5x + 13$ is _______
en.explanation:
A molecule has a permanent dipole moment $(\mu \neq 0)$ if its individual bond dipoles do not cancel each other out due to an unsymmetrical shape or the presence of lone pairs.

Set (a):

  • $\text{BeCl}_2$: Linear shape. The two equal $\text{Be}-\text{Cl}$ bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel out $(\mu = 0)$.

  • $\text{CO}_2$: Linear shape. The two equal $\text{C}=\text{O}$ bond dipoles cancel out $(\mu = 0)$.

  • $\text{BCl}_3$: Symmetrical trigonal planar geometry. The three bond dipoles cancel each other $(\mu = 0)$.

  • $\text{CHCl}_3$: Distorted tetrahedral geometry with different surrounding atoms. The bond dipoles do not cancel $(\mu \neq 0)$.

Set (b):

  • $\text{SO}_2$: Bent shape due to a lone pair on sulfur, so bond dipoles do not cancel $(\mu \neq 0)$.

  • $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$: Unsymmetrical planar structure with a polar $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond $(\mu \neq 0)$.

  • $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$: Bent shape with two lone pairs on selenium $(\mu \neq 0)$.

  • $\text{BrF}_5$: Square pyramidal geometry with one lone pair on bromine $(\mu \neq 0)$.

Set (c):

  • $\text{BF}_3$: Symmetrical trigonal planar geometry $(\mu = 0)$.

  • $\text{O}_3$: Angular (bent) geometry with resonance, leading to a net dipole moment $(\mu \neq 0)$.

  • $\text{SF}_6$: Symmetrical octahedral geometry $(\mu = 0)$.

  • $\text{XeF}_6$: Distorted octahedral geometry with one lone pair on xenon $(\mu \neq 0)$.

Set (d):

  • $\text{NO}_2$: Angular (bent) shape with an odd electron on nitrogen $(\mu \neq 0)$.

  • $\text{NH}_3$: Trigonal pyramidal shape with one lone pair on nitrogen $(\mu \neq 0)$.

  • $\text{POCl}_3$: Distorted tetrahedral geometry with different terminal atoms $(\mu \neq 0)$.

  • $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$: Distorted tetrahedral geometry $(\mu \neq 0)$.

The molecules possessing a permanent dipole moment are:

$\text{CHCl}_3$, $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$, $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$, $\text{BrF}_5$, $\text{O}_3$, $\text{XeF}_6$, $\text{NO}_2$, $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{POCl}_3$, and $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$.

Total number of polar molecules:

$$X = 11$$

Now, substituting the value of $X$:

$$5X + 13 = 5(11) + 13 = 55 + 13 = 68$$

68

en.content: A certain diatomic molecule AB has dipole moment 1.6 D and the internuclear distance is 100 pm. The fraction of electronic charge existing on more electronegative atom is
en.explanation:
For a diatomic molecule, dipole moment is given by

$$ \mu = q \times r $$

where $q$ is the charge separated and $r$ is the internuclear distance.

Here,

$$ \mu = 1.6 \, D $$

and

$$ r = 100 \, pm = 1 \, \mathring{A} $$

If one full electronic charge were separated by $1 \, \mathring{A}$, the dipole moment would be

$$ \mu = 4.8 \, D $$

So, the fraction of electronic charge present is

$$ \text{Fraction} = \frac{\text{observed dipole moment}}{\text{dipole moment for full charge separation}} $$

$$ = \frac{1.6}{4.8} $$

$$ = \frac{1}{3} $$

$$ = 0.33 $$

So, the fraction of electronic charge existing on the more electronegative atom is

$$ \boxed{0.33} $$

or about

$$ \boxed{33\%} $$
